parsed_answer.content:
In enterprise software engineering, maintaining a codebase that survives business pivots and technology churn requires rigorous structural discipline. Layered Architecture, Hexagonal Architecture (also known as Ports & Adapters), and Clean Architecture represent the evolutionary steps of separating concerns, isolating business domains from infrastructure dependencies, and protecting core logic from the volatile nature of databases, frameworks, and user interfaces.

Layered Architecture organizes code horizontally, traditionally dividing applications into Presentation, Business Logic, and Persistence layers. While straightforward, it suffers from a tendency where upper layers leak dependencies downward, often tightly coupling the domain model to Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) annotations and SQL schemas. Hexagonal Architecture, pioneered by Alistair Cockburn, redefines this layout geometrically. It places the domain at the center, surrounded by an application layer, and isolates them from the outside world using Ports (interfaces defining interactions) and Adapters (implementations bridging the ports to external technologies like REST controllers or JDBC repositories). This inversion of control ensures that the application core remains entirely agnostic of whether it is driven by a command-line interface, a REST API, or an automated test suite.

Clean Architecture, popularized by Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob), synthesizes these ideas into the Dependency Rule: source code dependencies must point only inward, toward higher-level policies and enterprise business rules. By structuring code into concentric circles representing Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks/Drivers, Clean Architecture guarantees that core business logic has zero knowledge of the external frameworks housing it. In Java ecosystems, implementing these architectural styles requires leveraging dependency injection frameworks like Spring or CDI carefully, ensuring that domain model classes do not import infrastructure-specific annotations, thereby maximizing testability, maintainability, and domain longevity.

items: In Hexagonal Architecture, Driving Ports (Primary Ports) represent use case interfaces invoked by external actors, while Driven Ports (Secondary Ports) represent interfaces implemented by infrastructure adapters to query databases or invoke external microservices.

The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) from SOLID is the mechanical backbone of Clean and Hexagonal architectures, allowing high-level business logic to define interfaces that low-level persistence or web frameworks must implement.

Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) and mappers are mandatory at architectural boundaries to prevent domain entities from leaking persistence framework proxies or JSON serialization annotations into the business core.

parsed_answer.content: A common production anti-pattern in Java when applying Clean or Hexagonal architectures is 'DTO-itis'—creating a distinct object for every single layer (RequestDTO, Command, DomainEntity, PersistenceEntity, ResponseDTO). This leads to excessive boilerplate mapping code that slows development without adding real domain resilience. Balance your mapping strategy; reuse domain models as persistence entities if your ORM usage is simple, but draw a hard boundary where external frameworks threaten domain purity.
